item.text: {"chapter_id":"3B","answers":[{"question_id":"3B.1","answer":"The record shows a mixed formal-practical picture, but implementation was materially inadequate. Positive evidence includes a constitutional framework requiring the National Guard to respect human rights and prohibiting torture and enforced disappearance, a 2023 legal framework with disciplinary procedures and sanctions, CNDH monitoring, and some government-supported search, identification, and truth mechanisms (BATCH-0055-E003; BATCH-0057-E014; BATCH-0057-E015; BATCH-0004-E003; BATCH-0015-E016). Adverse evidence is stronger for 2023 outcomes and implementation: arbitrary detention remained widespread; torture, disappearances, unlawful killings, poor detention conditions, and deficient detention records persisted; National Guard and military personnel were implicated in serious violations; and disappearance investigations and registry administration remained contested (BATCH-0049-E011; BATCH-0004-E004; BATCH-0004-E012; BATCH-0045-E002; BATCH-0045-E003; BATCH-0021-R01-E011; BATCH-0021-R01-E008). Ayotzinapa illustrates both an initial protective initiative and later failure to secure military cooperation, with the whereabouts of most students unresolved and independent investigators withdrawing (BATCH-0003-E015; BATCH-0003-E016; BATCH-0008-E002; BATCH-0013-E002; BATCH-0021-R02-E001). The Nuevo Laredo killings and allegations of scene manipulation and military-led investigation further qualify the record, although direct presidential orders and final individual liability are not established (BATCH-0010-E004; BATCH-0012-E012; BATCH-0049-E005; BATCH-0038-E003). The period fit is strongest for 2023 institutional findings; some disappearance and military-pattern evidence is inherited or spans earlier years. Attribution supports responsibility for the security model, deployments, and public responses, but not personal command of every abuse. Causation is therefore mixed and uncertainty remains about the full scale, final adjudication, and effectiveness of remedies.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0055-E003","BATCH-0057-E014","BATCH-0057-E015","BATCH-0004-E003","BATCH-0015-E016","BATCH-0003-E016","BATCH-0021-R01-E002"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0049-E011","BATCH-0004-E004","BATCH-0004-E012","BATCH-0045-E002","BATCH-0045-E003","BATCH-0021-R01-E011","BATCH-0021-R01-E008","BATCH-0010-E004","BATCH-0049-E005"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Formal safeguards are better documented than their enforcement.","Many abuses are attributed to institutions or subnational authorities rather than personally to López Obrador.","Several indicators span earlier years, and final judicial outcomes or complete remedy records are unavailable."]},{"question_id":"3B.2","answer":"López Obrador clearly appointed, funded, expanded, and politically defended coercive institutions, especially the National Guard and armed forces. Positive evidence includes extensive training and staffing, formal human-rights duties, disciplinary procedures, CNDH and UN oversight, and some cooperation with investigations (BATCH-0055-E011; BATCH-0055-E015; BATCH-0057-E014; BATCH-0057-E015; BATCH-0049-E011). The adverse implementation record is substantial: military personnel assumed broad civilian-security functions; military and National Guard forces were implicated in killings, arbitrary detention, torture, disappearances, excessive force, and unregistered arrests; referrals and sanctions were limited; and military institutions allegedly obstructed investigations (BATCH-0003-E006; BATCH-0003-E011; BATCH-0008-E008; BATCH-0009-E003; BATCH-0016-E005; BATCH-0016-E007; BATCH-0016-E010). The president defended military control even after the Supreme Court held the transfer of National Guard control unconstitutional, while the practical composition of the Guard remained overwhelmingly military (BATCH-0005-E001; BATCH-0009-E004; BATCH-0016-E002; BATCH-0031-E013). Individual presidential authorization of particular abuses is not established; the attribution is principally policy-level, command-environment, appointment, resource, and response responsibility. Positive training and oversight measures therefore coexist with a security architecture that expanded discretion faster than demonstrated accountability.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0055-E011","BATCH-0055-E015","BATCH-0057-E014","BATCH-0057-E015","BATCH-0049-E011","BATCH-0016-E007"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0003-E006","BATCH-0003-E011","BATCH-0008-E008","BATCH-0009-E003","BATCH-0016-E005","BATCH-0016-E010","BATCH-0005-E001","BATCH-0031-E013"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Security-force conduct is decentralized and not every incident is traceable to presidential orders.","Some training and staffing figures come from official or dissenting accounts and do not establish training quality.","Sanction and investigation data are incomplete and sometimes advocacy-based."]},{"question_id":"3B.3","answer":"The evidence does not support a finding that López Obrador consistently avoided stigmatizing or threatening rhetoric. He repeatedly attacked journalists, civil-society organizations, feminists, environmental defenders, opposition demonstrators, and critics, including through recurring presidential briefings and the 'Who's Who in Lies' segment (BATCH-0004-E014; BATCH-0007-E005; BATCH-0012-E008; BATCH-0012-E015; BATCH-0029-E006; BATCH-0044-E012). Reports document intimidation, harassment, threats, doxing, online abuse, and some private attacks echoing presidential language, but do not prove that he personally ordered physical attacks or killings (BATCH-0012-E008; BATCH-0029-E006; BATCH-0047-E008; BATCH-0026-E016). There is limited favorable or qualifying evidence: formal free-expression protections remained, independent media and online mobilization persisted, and the president sometimes stated that opposition and free expression were legitimate (BATCH-0004-E014; BATCH-0026-E018; BATCH-0014-E001; BATCH-0012-E012). However, the conduct, implementation, and effects point to official stigmatization and inadequate action against resulting threats rather than restraint or effective correction. The rhetoric is directly attributable to the ruler; subsequent violence has mixed state, criminal, and unidentified causation. The strongest evidence concerns journalists and civic actors, with less direct evidence regarding migrants or ethnic minorities.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0004-E014","BATCH-0007-E005","BATCH-0012-E008","BATCH-0012-E015","BATCH-0029-E006","BATCH-0044-E012"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0026-E018","BATCH-0014-E001","BATCH-0012-E012","BATCH-0029-E006","BATCH-0047-E008"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Rhetorical influence on individual threats is reported but not finally adjudicated.","Criminal and local actors account for part of the violence.","The candidate index contains stronger evidence on journalists and defenders than on all protected groups."]},{"question_id":"3B.4","answer":"Independent oversight and complaint institutions existed and sometimes operated, but executive and military conduct repeatedly limited their effectiveness and remedy. Positive evidence includes CNDH complaint processing, recommendations, criminal referrals, prison and migration inspections, UN access, judicial review, National Search Commission initiatives, truth-commission activity, and Supreme Court invalidation of unconstitutional security arrangements (BATCH-0021-R01-E002; BATCH-0021-R01-E003; BATCH-0021-R01-E004; BATCH-0021-R01-E009; BATCH-0049-E011; BATCH-0004-E003; BATCH-0009-E004). The UN and courts were able to identify legal and institutional violations, and some officials were investigated or convicted (BATCH-0004-E012; BATCH-0049-E005; BATCH-0046-E010). Adverse evidence shows widespread impunity, weak prosecutorial resolution, CNDH recommendations with incomplete acceptance or compliance, paralysis of INAI, attacks on courts and critics, military noncooperation in Ayotzinapa, and disputed manipulation of disappearance data (BATCH-0003-E010; BATCH-0021-R01-E008; BATCH-0021-R01-E009; BATCH-0047-E013; BATCH-0013-E002; BATCH-0004-E008). López Obrador initiated some mechanisms but did not reliably compel military or executive compliance and publicly discredited victims, journalists, courts, and investigators (BATCH-0003-E016; BATCH-0004-E007; BATCH-0009-E007). Attribution is strongest for executive pressure, appointments, security policy, and failure to enforce cooperation, while individual obstruction often remains institutionally rather than personally attributed.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0021-R01-E002","BATCH-0021-R01-E003","BATCH-0021-R01-E004","BATCH-0021-R01-E009","BATCH-0049-E011","BATCH-0004-E003","BATCH-0009-E004"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0003-E010","BATCH-0021-R01-E008","BATCH-0047-E013","BATCH-0013-E002","BATCH-0004-E008","BATCH-0003-E016","BATCH-0004-E007"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Acceptance of recommendations is not equivalent to remedy.","Many oversight outcomes concern state and local authorities beyond direct presidential control.","Some evidence is institutional self-reporting or advocacy assessment rather than final adjudication."]},{"question_id":"3B.5","answer":"The administration used exceptional security, military, detention, and surveillance powers broadly, with important judicial constraints but limited evidence of voluntary narrow administration or prompt correction. Formal safeguards existed: judicial authorization requirements for communications interception, time limits and inventories, detention registries, civilian jurisdiction principles, and constitutional limits on military assistance (BATCH-0057-E007; BATCH-0057-E012; BATCH-0055-E012; BATCH-0055-E013). The Supreme Court invalidated the transfer of National Guard control to Defense and an undercover-operation power, while the UN and Inter-American system criticized mandatory pretrial detention and arraigo (BATCH-0055-E006; BATCH-0057-E006; BATCH-0049-E011; BATCH-0004-E009). Against this, the executive expanded permanent military participation, defended military control after the ruling, tolerated unregistered military arrests, maintained arraigo and mandatory detention, and failed to resolve allegations of unlawful Pegasus surveillance and data-access abuses (BATCH-0005-E001; BATCH-0008-E010; BATCH-0009-E003; BATCH-0014-E006; BATCH-0014-E007; BATCH-0026-E019). The president’s public defense of military intelligence and minimization of surveillance allegations are directly attributable; operational surveillance and detention abuses are attributed to security institutions with uncertain personal authorization. The period fit is strong for 2023 judicial and oversight findings, while several surveillance practices began earlier.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0057-E007","BATCH-0057-E012","BATCH-0055-E012","BATCH-0055-E013","BATCH-0055-E006","BATCH-0057-E006"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0005-E001","BATCH-0008-E010","BATCH-0009-E003","BATCH-0014-E006","BATCH-0014-E007","BATCH-0026-E019","BATCH-0004-E009"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Some powers were legally constrained only prospectively or remained unresolved.","Surveillance allegations are not uniformly supported by final judicial findings.","The index does not establish complete compliance after the Supreme Court ruling."]},{"question_id":"3B.6","answer":"Mexico experienced some reduction in homicide and selected property-crime indicators, but the reduction was modest, remained contested, and was accompanied by severe organized-crime, disappearance, extortion, and state-abuse risks. Positive evidence includes a 2023 homicide decline, a fourth consecutive annual peacefulness improvement, lower reported crime from 2018 to 2023, and reductions in some theft categories (BATCH-0003-E003; BATCH-0004-E019; BATCH-0016-E009). The government claimed broader reductions, and some analyses report fewer armed confrontations or lower absolute levels of certain violations (BATCH-0007-E004; BATCH-0047-E009). Contrary evidence is substantial: more than 30,500 killings occurred in 2023; organized-crime violence remained severe; political killings reached a record; homicides rose from 2022 to 2023 in one analysis; extortion and other offenses increased; impunity remained above 90%; and military expansion did not reliably explain subnational homicide reductions (BATCH-0004-E019; BATCH-0016-E008; BATCH-0016-E010; BATCH-0016-E011; BATCH-0051-E017). State violence, torture, arbitrary detention, and alleged extrajudicial killings qualify any safety gain (BATCH-0049-E011; BATCH-0016-E005; BATCH-0010-E004). Attribution to López Obrador is strongest for the militarized strategy and resource allocation, but organized crime, inherited institutional weakness, measurement changes, and external firearms supply complicate causation.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0003-E003","BATCH-0004-E019","BATCH-0016-E009","BATCH-0007-E004","BATCH-0047-E009"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0004-E019","BATCH-0016-E008","BATCH-0016-E010","BATCH-0016-E011","BATCH-0051-E017","BATCH-0049-E011","BATCH-0016-E005","BATCH-0010-E004"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Official crime statistics may be affected by classification and undercounting.","The candidate index does not provide a complete exposure-adjusted national violence series.","Non-state criminal violence and inherited conditions limit causal attribution."]},{"question_id":"3B.7","answer":"The administration enacted and supported several protective legal and service measures, but implementation was uneven and serious violence, displacement, discrimination, and neglect persisted. Positive evidence includes expanded same-sex marriage and gender recognition, disability-rights reforms, gender-violence laws and training, migrant-child protection programs, expanded asylum and COMAR capacity, shelters, child-protection routes, and UN-supported services (BATCH-0004-E013; BATCH-0015-E004; BATCH-0015-E016; BATCH-0015-E017; BATCH-0015-E012). The UN also documented 2023 cooperation on gender violence, mobility, shelters, and protection (BATCH-0015-E011; BATCH-0015-E016). Adverse evidence includes persistent femicide, gender violence, disappearances, migrant detention abuse and deaths, overloaded shelters, unequal access, Indigenous and disability-related exclusion, and inadequate implementation of child-protection protocols (BATCH-0051-E009; BATCH-0004-E006; BATCH-0015-E007; BATCH-0015-E017; BATCH-0049-E011). Legal reforms often came through Congress, courts, UN agencies, or subnational actors rather than personal presidential direction. The president’s migration-enforcement and militarization policies are more directly attributable, while local policing and service failures require caution. Outcomes therefore show partial institutional protection without equitable or reliable nationwide safety.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0004-E013","BATCH-0015-E004","BATCH-0015-E016","BATCH-0015-E017","BATCH-0015-E012","BATCH-0015-E011"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0051-E009","BATCH-0004-E006","BATCH-0015-E007","BATCH-0049-E011","BATCH-0015-E017"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Many positive measures are legal or programmatic inputs rather than demonstrated outcomes.","Subnational implementation and external UN support complicate presidential attribution.","Evidence is stronger for women, children, migrants, and journalists than for all minorities and vulnerable groups."]},{"question_id":"3B.8","answer":"Formal rights to assembly, speech, association, and internet access remained in place, and courts continued to provide some protection, but actual protest and dissent were exposed to stigmatization, surveillance, criminalization, excessive force, and weak remedy. Positive evidence includes formal constitutional protections, active independent media, robust online mobilization, judicial review of restrictive measures, and some accountability mechanisms (BATCH-0004-E014; BATCH-0026-E018; BATCH-0014-E001; BATCH-0057-E014). Adverse evidence includes hundreds of documented press attacks, state-attributed aggression, excessive force and arbitrary detention at protests, criminal proceedings against defenders, military Pegasus surveillance, presidential attacks on journalists and demonstrators, and continuing impunity (BATCH-0012-E007; BATCH-0012-E008; BATCH-0010-E007; BATCH-0030-E001; BATCH-0029-E006; BATCH-0044-E012). At least some private abuse reportedly echoed presidential rhetoric, but physical violence was also committed by criminal and local actors, so direct causation is not established (BATCH-0012-E008; BATCH-0041-E006). The ruler is directly attributable for repeated stigmatizing rhetoric, surveillance defenses, military deployment policy, and inadequate national protection posture; individual local policing incidents are not automatically attributable.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0004-E014","BATCH-0026-E018","BATCH-0014-E001","BATCH-0057-E014","BATCH-0012-E007","BATCH-0012-E008"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0010-E007","BATCH-0030-E001","BATCH-0029-E006","BATCH-0044-E012","BATCH-0041-E006"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Documented attacks may undercount total violence.","Many protest incidents are state-level or local.","Formal legal protection and actual enforcement are not equivalent."]},{"question_id":"3B.9","answer":"Crisis responses combined genuine mobilization and coordination with delays, military-centered administration, contested information, and uneven protection. Positive evidence includes substantial military and government deployment after Hurricane Otis, humanitarian and reconstruction coordination, emergency worktables, shelter, health, food, and communications support, and CNDH intervention in affected prisons (BATCH-0003-E022; BATCH-0015-E015; BATCH-0015-E012; BATCH-0015-E015; BATCH-0021-R01-E013). The administration also issued formal prevention, human-rights, and emergency-policy frameworks (BATCH-0044-E011; BATCH-0055-E012). Adverse evidence includes reports that aid reached some residents only after delays, shortages of food, water, medicine, gasoline, and communications, insufficient assistance to poorer residents, early presidential claims minimizing casualty criticism, and military control that reduced transparency in prior disaster responses (BATCH-0031-E003; BATCH-0050-E010; BATCH-0029-E003; BATCH-0018-E007). Ayotzinapa and Nuevo Laredo show crisis and security responses marked by contested narratives, institutional obstruction, or disputed investigations (BATCH-0013-E002; BATCH-0049-E005). The Otis response is directly period-fitted but early snapshots cannot establish final recovery or distributional equity. López Obrador is attributable for public messaging, deployment choices, and federal coordination, while delays and local failures have mixed causation.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0003-E022","BATCH-0015-E015","BATCH-0015-E012","BATCH-0021-R01-E013","BATCH-0044-E011","BATCH-0055-E012"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0031-E003","BATCH-0050-E010","BATCH-0029-E003","BATCH-0018-E007","BATCH-0013-E002","BATCH-0049-E005"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Most disaster evidence is an early response snapshot.","Long-term recovery and equitable allocation are not established.","Some evidence concerns earlier crises and provides contextual rather than direct 2023 proof."]},{"question_id":"3B.10","answer":"The evidence does not establish that López Obrador left Mexico durably safer overall. There were some favorable outcomes: homicide and selected crime measures declined from parts of the inherited baseline, peacefulness improved modestly in 2023, poverty and inequality improved, and some protection, search, asylum, and oversight capacities expanded (BATCH-0003-E003; BATCH-0004-E019; BATCH-0016-E009; BATCH-0015-E009; BATCH-0015-E016; BATCH-0015-E017). However, severe contrary outcomes persisted or worsened: more than 30,500 people were killed in 2023, disappearances exceeded 110,000, organized-crime and political violence remained severe, impunity remained pervasive, journalists and defenders continued to be killed, arbitrary detention and military abuses persisted, and institutional capacity and civilian oversight weakened (BATCH-0004-E019; BATCH-0045-E002; BATCH-0045-E003; BATCH-0016-E010; BATCH-0016-E012; BATCH-0012-E007; BATCH-0049-E011). The administration’s central contribution was a durable expansion of military authority and resources, but evidence that this caused the limited crime improvements is weak or contradicted by subnational analysis (BATCH-0016-E007; BATCH-0016-E011). Reporting freedom remained sufficient to reveal abuse, though repression and criminal threats also produced underreporting and self-censorship (BATCH-0014-E001; BATCH-0012-E007). The inherited baseline was already highly violent and institutionally weak; external firearms supply and organized-crime fragmentation further limit causal attribution. End-state safety therefore appears mixed, with modest selected improvements offset by persistent severe violence, state-abuse risks, and weaker accountability.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0003-E003","BATCH-0004-E019","BATCH-0016-E009","BATCH-0015-E009","BATCH-0015-E016","BATCH-0015-E017"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0004-E019","BATCH-0045-E002","BATCH-0045-E003","BATCH-0016-E010","BATCH-0016-E012","BATCH-0012-E007","BATCH-0049-E011","BATCH-0016-E011"],"limitations_and_gaps":["There is no complete counterfactual or exposure-adjusted national safety estimate.","Several end-state indicators combine federal, state, criminal, and inherited causes.","Open reporting improves visibility but does not eliminate underreporting or self-censorship."]}],"cross_lens_observations":["Across the ten lenses, formal safeguards, oversight bodies, training, search mechanisms, legal reforms, and selected crime improvements coexist with persistent torture, arbitrary detention, disappearances, military and National Guard abuses, journalist and defender violence, weak remedy, and expanded military discretion.","The strongest ruler attribution concerns the decision to expand and politically defend military involvement in civilian security, public rhetoric toward critics, surveillance posture, and failure to compel military cooperation. Individual killings, local policing, criminal violence, and many service failures require more limited attribution.","Evidence is strongest for 2023 institutional findings and outcomes, while several baseline comparisons and surveillance or disappearance patterns span earlier years. Formal laws and institutional creation are materially more favorable than documented implementation and remedy.","The information environment was open enough for substantial independent reporting and judicial review, but censorship-like pressure, stigmatization, surveillance, criminal threats, and self-censorship mean that low complaint or reporting volumes cannot be treated as evidence of safety."]}
